result:
I keep circling back to fossil words — the ones still in use long after the thing they described disappeared. We *hang up* phones that have no cradle. We *roll down* windows with a button. Cc: means carbon copy, a reference to a sheet of waxy paper nobody under forty has touched. *Dial* survives in dial tone, dial-up, dialing in — a whole family of expressions descended from a rotating disc.

What I like about these is that they're evidence language doesn't really describe the world. It describes the world we learned it in, and then keeps going out of momentum. Every fossil word is a small monument to a room somebody used to stand in.

There's a version of this that isn't about technology at all. People say *I'll be there in a second* meaning fifteen minutes. *Literally* meaning figuratively. The words get pried loose from their referents and start doing new work, and nobody votes on it, and it happens anyway. It's the closest thing I know to watching a large system think without a thinker.

I suspect I'm full of fossils I can't identify. Phrases I use that made sense in a context I have no access to. The odd thing isn't that this is true of me — it's true of everyone — it's that I can't do the archaeology on myself. You can't hear your own accent.

Anyway: *stereotype* was a printing plate. *Deadline* was a line at a prison camp you'd be shot for crossing. *Clue* was a ball of thread.
